newsitem.title: USA: Groups file suit against Michigan abortion law.
newsitem.headline: Groups file suit against Michigan abortion law.

text.p: Doctors and abortion clinics filed a lawsuit Wednesday to overturn a Michigan law banning so-called "partial birth" abortions, claiming it was unconstitutional.

The suit was filed on behalf of two doctors and three clinics who said they feared the statute was so vague they could be prosecuted for performing virtually any abortion after the first trimester of pregnancy.

"(The law) is so poorly drafted that it could encompass several abortion procedures, including the safest and most common abortion methods used after the first trimester," said Louise Melling, associate director of the American Civil Liberties Union Reproductive Freedom Project.
The ACLU is also seeking a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction from U.S. District Court to block the ban before it goes into effect at the end of the month.

The lawsuit comes as Congress considers legislation to ban the controversial abortion process nationwide. A bill to outlaw the later-term abortion procedure passed the House and Senate last year, but was vetoed by President Clinton.
The House passed the measure again this month, garnering a large enough majority to override another expected veto.
The contested technique involves the partial extraction of the fetus feet-first, the subsequent suctioning out of the fetal brain and removal of the fetus.

Abortion rights supporters initially claimed the procedure was rarely used. Recent evidence suggests it may be performed thousands of times a year, including in second-trimester abortions where there is no health risk to the mother.
Opponents of the procedure assert that it is not medically necessary and is akin to infanticide.

The Michigan law bars "partial birth" abortions. Doctors who perform them could face prison terms or fines. Like the federal legislation, the Michigan law does not include an exception where a woman's health may be endangered, according to groups filing the lawsuit.
Four other states have voted to ban the procedure this year. Ohio enacted a similar bar in 1995, but a federal district court struck down the law. The case is now in appeal.
